title: Dirac Delta Function
body:
$\delta(x)$ is the idealised impulse: zero everywhere except $x = 0$, infinite there, and with
$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta(x)\,dx = 1$. **It is not a function**, strictly. No function has
those properties; it is a distribution, defined by what it does inside an integral rather than by
its values. Treat it as the limit of a spike that gets taller and narrower while keeping unit area.

Everything you need follows from the sifting property:

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,\delta(x - a)\,dx = f(a)
$$

Integrating against $\delta$ **samples** $f$ at one point, which is exactly what an ADC does at one
instant. A train of deltas spaced $T$ apart (a Dirac comb) is the idealised model of sampling a
whole signal, and that model is how [[Sampling Theorem]] is proved.

Two facts to keep. It is the identity for convolution, $f * \delta = f$, so shifting a delta and
convolving delays a signal without changing it (see [[Convolution Theorem]]). And its
[[Fourier Transform]] is the constant 1: **an instantaneous strike contains every frequency
equally**, which is why hitting something sharply makes a click rather than a note, and why the
comb's transform is another comb.

Physically it models an instant strike: a hammer blow starting a [[Wave Equation]] solution, a point
charge, a shock load. See [[Partial Differential Equations]] in [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]].
